question: Describe the electromagnetic spectrum. Explain why there is no sharp boundary between two neighbouring regions of the spectrum. Support your answer by mentioning the sources and uses of four different regions of the spectrum.

options.A:
The electromagnetic spectrum is the arrangement of electromagnetic waves according to amplitude. It has sharp boundaries because each type has a completely separate wavelength range.
Radio waves are emitted by radioactive nuclei and used in cancer therapy; microwaves are produced by hot bodies and used in thermal imaging; infrared rays are produced by klystrons and used in X-ray diagnosis; X-rays are produced by vibrating circuits and used for radio communication.
options.B:
The electromagnetic spectrum is the arrangement of electromagnetic waves according to energy only. Adjacent regions have no boundary because all waves have the same wavelength.
Radio waves are produced by hot bodies and used for sterilisation; microwaves are produced by nuclei and used in X-ray imaging; infrared rays are produced by stopped electrons and used in radar; X-rays are produced by conducting wires and used in remote controls.
options.C:
The electromagnetic spectrum contains radio waves, microwaves, infrared rays, visible light, ultraviolet rays, X-rays and gamma rays. The regions have sharp boundaries fixed solely by their sources.
Radio waves are produced by accelerated charges in wires and used for communication; microwaves are produced by magnetrons and used in radar; infrared is emitted by hot bodies and used in thermal imaging; X-rays are produced by stopped electrons and used in diagnosis.
options.D:
The electromagnetic spectrum is the orderly arrangement of electromagnetic waves according to wavelength or frequency. It includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared rays, visible light, ultraviolet rays, X-rays and gamma rays.
There is no sharp boundary between neighbouring regions because their wavelength/frequency ranges can overlap; the divisions are mainly based on methods of production and detection.
Radio waves are produced by accelerated charges in conducting wires and used for radio/TV communication; microwaves are produced by klystrons or magnetrons and used in radar or ovens; infrared rays are emitted by hot bodies and used in remote controls or thermal imaging; X-rays are produced when high-energy electrons are stopped by a metal target and used in medical diagnosis or crystal studies.
